title: It's the Final Countdown
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Opening his March article series, Dave Stuart Jr. examines the practice of counting down to the end of the school year, arguing it can be either corrosive or clarifying depending on how it's framed. He concedes that a careless countdown can damage a teacher's Credibility and the Value of the class by signaling to students that the time together is something to be survived rather than something meaningful. But he argues counting down can also be an expression of wisdom, invoking the Psalmist's 'teach us to number our days' and Oliver Burkeman's '4,000 weeks' to frame finite time as something to use consciously rather than something to dread. His preferred version of a countdown produces what he calls 'gentle urgency' — an awareness that class time is precious and connected to the school year's actual ending, which should shape how the time is used rather than how eagerly it's anticipated. He closes by previewing a 'final quarter countdown' framework of beginning, middle, and end phases that will structure his articles through the rest of March.
points: A careless end-of-year countdown can damage both Credibility and the Value belief by signaling, even unintentionally, that class time is something to survive rather than something worthwhile.
Counting down responsibly is reframed as an act of wisdom rather than burnout, anchored in the Psalmist's 'teach us to number our days' and Oliver Burkeman's finite '4,000 weeks' framing.
The concept of 'gentle urgency' names the specific, productive version of time-awareness Stuart is after: precious, finite, but not crass or dismissive of the work still ahead.
Framing the school year into three phases — first 90 days, middle days, final 90 days — sets up a structural lens for deciding what kind of work makes sense at each stage.

Stuart's honest admission that he does count down, paired with his caveat that it can hurt as well as help, models the kind of nuanced self-reflection he's asking readers to bring to their own practice.
quotes: When we count down in this manner, it becomes a crass endeavor. We end up (perhaps accidentally) saying, "What we do here isn't important. It's something to be survived, to get through — nothing more.
Teach us to number our days," the Psalmist writes, "that we may get a heart of wisdom.
You'll know you're doing the countdown right when it helps you craft the semi-paradoxical classroom state that I call "gentle urgency.

A countdown like this can help you and your students orient around the reality that class time is precious, that human lifespans are finite, and that even in March, the time we're given is connected to those last days of school that are coming in May or June.
The work we do now, in other words, directly affects who we'll be then. So let's use the time wisely.
